title: The Shared Decision at Riverside Theatre
author: ONE HOME original short-reader collection
pages: Asha arrived at Riverside Theatre before the afternoon activity began. The room was quiet, but there was plenty to prepare. On a small table lay a folder, ready to be used. Then the organiser explained the difficulty: two groups wanted to use the same space. Asha had expected a simple afternoon and felt uncertain. Instead of pretending to know the answer, Asha asked for a few minutes to look carefully. There was still time to understand what had happened before anyone made a decision.

The first step was to listen to both groups and look at the booking sheet. This took longer than making a quick guess, but it gave the group something useful to work with. Asha wrote down what was known and put a question mark beside what still needed checking. A friend suggested rushing ahead. “If we get the first part wrong, we may have to do everything twice,” Asha replied. Together they compared the information. One detail mattered more than the others: a plan had to work for the people who would actually use it.

Soon the group had a possible answer. They could agree a timetable that gave each group a turn. Asha explained the idea, then asked the others what might go wrong. At first, nobody spoke. After a moment, a younger visitor raised a concern. The group listened rather than dismissing it. They changed a small part of the plan and tried it on a limited scale. The trial was not perfect, but it showed them what to improve. Asha used a folder to keep track of the next step.

When the visitors arrived, the group put the revised plan into practice. Someone who had missed the discussion asked why they had chosen this approach. Asha explained both the problem and the reason for the decision. That explanation helped the newcomer take part without feeling left behind. During the afternoon, the team checked how things were going. They did not assume that silence meant success. They asked people directly and made another small adjustment when it was needed.

By the end of the afternoon, Riverside Theatre felt different. The original problem had become a chance to practise being fair. Asha returned a folder to the table and wrote a note for the next group: “Check, listen, try, then improve.” The organiser thanked everyone, including the visitor whose question had changed the plan. Asha was pleased, but the best part was knowing how the group had reached its answer. They had not needed one person to know everything. They had needed people who were willing to think together.

questions.prompt: What difficulty did the group face?
choices: new visitors found the entrance difficult to locate
two groups wanted to use the same space
a box of donated objects had lost its labels
the planned activity left quieter visitors with no way to join
questions.hint: Look back at what the group actually did.

questions.prompt: What did the group decide to do?
choices: write labels that explained where each object came from
add simple signs at the confusing turning points
agree a timetable that gave each group a turn
invite people to choose how they wanted to take part

questions.prompt: Why did the group test a small version first?
choices: To discover problems before using the full plan
To make the task last forever
